proof.caseStudy: /case-studies/nitro/ (content/case-studies/nitro.md). The ONLY gaming proof. No other gaming client may be claimed or implied.
supports: Nitro League is a decentralised play-to-earn (P2E) racing game powered by upgradeable NFTs and the Nitro token, built for 3 audiences: gamers, NFT collectors and investors.
Scope (quote exactly): idea to product, conceptualisation, art direction, sketching and modeling, MVP launch plan, game and website design, and post-launch enhancements.

Experiences designed: a 2D simulation game (core racing loop), an immersive 3D garage where players inspect, upgrade and show off cars and the community gathers, a lineup of race-ready cars designed to read as collectibles, a marketing website (game, roadmap, whitepaper, tokenomics) that leads players and investors into the NFT marketplace, and a garage and cars collection UI shown on a mobile screen.

Method: product discovery and stakeholder interviews, then user flows and a detailed whitepaper, then branding workshops for the visual identity. CG artists visualised the gameplay, design thinking shaped the garage and the website, and professional gamers validated the result.
Tokenomics and IDO launch screens were designed (image caption 'Tokenomics and IDO launch design').
Result (quote exactly): secured $5M in funding within 3 months. Also: strategic NFT sales spread awareness, and the upgradeable NFTs came with 3D and AR/VR visuals.
doesNotSupport: Engine work (Unity, Unreal or any code), game programming, porting, multiplayer or netcode.
Art production at scale (full asset pipelines, animation, VFX, character rigs). The case says 'art direction' and 'sketching and modeling' only. Repeat those words, never expand them.
Console or PC titles, console certification (TRC/XR/Lotcheck), platform submission, game QA or bug testing, live-ops management.
Designing the token economics or setting the allocation numbers. Say we designed the tokenomics and IDO launch screens. Do not reprint the allocation table as our design decision.
Building AR/VR experiences (the result line says the NFTs 'came with 3D and AR/VR visuals'; do not say we built AR/VR).
Attributing the $5M to design alone. Write it as the project's reported result.
Any count of games shipped, game studio clients, player numbers, retention or DAU uplifts, or awards for gaming.
proof.otherCaseStudies: Parents Connect (/case-studies/parents-connect/) designed community patterns (forums, follow, real-time chat, reactions, events calendar; +45% forum participation). Use it at most once, as 'outside games, the same community patterns…', never called a game or gaming client. Optional. Skip it if the section runs over 70 words. No other case study is relevant.

outline.h2: Which game screens do our game UI/UX design services cover?
outline.answerHint: Bold: 6 parts of a game. One item per child with a concrete example.
points: Heads-up display (HUD): health, speed, map, timers readable at a glance during motion
Menus and settings: main menu, pause, controls remapping, audio and subtitle settings
First-time user experience (FTUE): the first session, from launch to the first win, teaching controls in play
Inventory and garage screens: compare, upgrade and equip items (Nitro's 3D garage and cars collection)
In-game store: currencies, bundles, battle pass, loot box odds shown before purchase
Game website and marketplace: roadmap, whitepaper, NFT marketplace (Nitro)

outline.h2: What makes UX design for games different from app UX?
outline.answerHint: Bold: UI UX design for games makes the challenge fun and removes friction everywhere else, so players struggle with the game, not the interface. 4 cards.
points: Intended challenge vs interface friction
Readability in motion: HUD contrast and size during play
Input variety: touch, controller and keyboard (mobile game UI design sizes thumb zones; the Apple Human Interface Guidelines cover game controls)
Trust in the game economy: prices, currencies and P2E rewards that players and investors believe (Nitro's investor-trust challenge)

outline.h2: How does our game UI/UX design process work?
outline.answerHint: Bold: game UI/UX design services take 8–16 weeks (40–80 working days) in 5 steps, from discovery to engine-ready handoff. Use the parent hub's 5 step names and day ranges, with game examples.
points: Discovery and product strategy (5–10 days): stakeholder interviews, core loop, audiences, success metrics
User research (5–15 days): interviews with target players, review of competitor games

outline.answerHint: Bold: these answers cover the 5 questions game studios ask most about game UI/UX design services.
points: see faqs[]

faqs.q: Do you build the game UI in Unity or Unreal Engine?
faqs.a: No. Game UI/UX design services deliver Figma screens, specifications and sliced UI assets, and the studio's Unity engine or Unreal Engine developers build them. (Matches the hub's 'designers do not write code'.)

faqs.q: Can you redesign the UI of a game that is already live?
faqs.a: Yes. Start with an audit of the live game ($5,000–$15,000, 2–3 weeks): store, FTUE and menu flows reviewed against player reviews and analytics, then a UI sprint.

faqs.q: Is game UI design outsourcing possible for only the HUD and menus?
faqs.a: Yes. A UI sprint ($25,000–$60,000, 4–8 weeks) covers 1–2 surfaces, for example the HUD and menus, with a playtested prototype.

faqs.q: Do you design mobile game UI for iOS and Android?
faqs.a: Yes. Mobile game UI design follows the Apple Human Interface Guidelines and Google Play policies, with touch targets of 44×44 pt on iOS and 48×48 dp on Android (mobile hub figures).

faqs.q: Have you designed a web3 or play-to-earn game?
faqs.a: Yes. Nitro League, a play-to-earn racing game with an NFT marketplace and a 3D garage; link /case-studies/nitro/. One project. Do not pluralise.
